# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review of Varga and Holm's Re-examination of the Halden Pilot

This comment does two different things, and they deserve different verdicts.

- **Sections 1–5 are valuable and mostly sound.** Using the pilot's own microdata, they confirm and put numbers on the problems I raised in the first review: attrition, manager-reported output, scheduled hours, nominal revenue, and the per-hour metric. They also add new facts, most importantly that the withdrawals happened *after* the schedule began.
- **Sections 6–8 overreach.** The headline conclusion, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact", is contradicted by the comment's own corrected estimate. It also depends on citing the Varden trial selectively.

The arithmetic in Table 2 checks out. For example, 95.4 / 0.861 gives +10.8%, and 1.014 / 1.041 gives −2.6% in real revenue. However, one set of figures does not reconcile, and the abstract describes corrections the paper never makes.

## 1. Internal inconsistencies

**The hours components don't add up.** The authors attribute the smaller fall in hours to two sources:
- 0.7 extra hours per day on the four remaining days, which is 2.8 hours a week;
- 1.6 hours a week logged on the day off.

Starting from 32 scheduled hours, that gives about **36.4 hours a week**. Starting from the baseline day of about 8.06 hours, it gives about 36.6. The reported pilot average is **34.6**. Either one of the two components is wrong, or "+0.7 hours per day" means something other than it appears to. This matters because these figures are the paper's main evidence for *why* actual hours fell by less than scheduled hours.

**The abstract says attrition was corrected, but it wasn't.** The abstract says that "correcting the first three" problems (attrition, output and hours) brings the gain down to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is described in Section 1 but never adjusted for. A bounding exercise would have been straightforward and informative. For example: what does the pooled gain become if the nine organisations that withdrew had zero gain per hour (an output index of 80)? The authors recommend analysing all enrolled organisations but don't attempt it themselves.

**Revenue doesn't belong in the list of causes.** The abstract counts four problems that "account for most of the reported gain". Revenue played no part in calculating the per-hour gain, so correcting it cannot reduce that gain.

## 2. The "entirely an artifact" conclusion doesn't follow

**The comment's own best estimate is a positive gain.** After correcting output and hours, the authors' figure is **+10.8%**, with no confidence interval reported. Getting from there to "entirely an artifact" rests on just two arguments:
- attrition, which is never quantified;
- novelty, which is inferred, not measured (see section 3 below).

Neither can carry an 11-point gain down to zero on the evidence given.

**It ignores the half of the Varden trial that cuts against it.** The comment calls Varden's counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature". That same trial, with the same randomised design, record-based output, timesheet hours and nine-month follow-up, found **+12.5% output per actual hour in case-processing offices (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)**. Varden has none of the problems the comment identifies in Halden: no manager-rated output, no scheduled-hours denominator, and a control group, which deals with general economic conditions. Yet the comment's conclusion covers "reduced-hours schemes" in general. Citing the stratum that supports its thesis and omitting the stratum that contradicts it is selective.

**The Data note contradicts the conclusion.** The Data note correctly says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." The conclusion then generalises to all reduced-hours schemes. Those two positions can't both stand.

**The corrected subset is probably mostly knowledge work.** The 17 organisations with both output records and time-tracking are likely weighted toward software and professional services. That is the kind of work where Varden *did* find a gain. So the 10.8% figure arguably supports a real effect in that kind of work rather than undermining it.

## 3. The novelty argument is weak, and the data to test it properly already exist

- **The extrapolation is off and thinly based.** Energy fell 0.32 SD over the three months between month three and month six. Projecting that decline in a straight line reaches zero at about **month 8.7**, not "around month ten". More fundamentally, a straight line drawn through two survey points is not a basis for prediction.
- **Energy is not output.** A falling self-reported mood score doesn't show that productivity is falling.
- **The direct test was available and not run.** The pilot collected the output index *monthly*. If the gain is a novelty effect, output per hour should decline from month one to month six, and the microdata can show whether it did. Given that the authors had the microdata, leaving this out is a notable gap.
- **The available evidence on duration cuts the other way.** Varden still found per-hour gains at nine months, longer than Halden's six. That doesn't rule out novelty, but it is evidence the comment doesn't engage with.
- **"The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter"** is a rhetorical move. It doesn't support a positive claim that the effect is entirely an artifact.

## 4. The critique of the meetings analysis misdescribes the Varden paper

- **"Selected for analysis after the results were known"** is inaccurate. Varden says the meeting data were collected in month six at managers' request, which was *before* the nine-month results.
- **It is not a hand-picked subgroup.** The seven offices are *all* the treated case-processing offices, a stratum fixed before randomisation.
- **It overlooks the strongest part of the evidence.** The 3.8 v 7.1 hours of meetings is a comparison between randomised treated and control offices. The r = 0.71 correlation across seven offices is weak, and the comment is right about that. The difference in meeting time between the two arms is more solid.
- **It treats the Varden authors as overclaiming when they didn't.** The Varden authors themselves said the analysis was unregistered, rested on seven offices, could not establish a mechanism, and would be tested in a registered confirmatory analysis.

There is also a tension in the comment's argument. If the meetings explanation is right, the per-hour gain is *real*: low-value time was removed and output was maintained. Dismissing the meetings hypothesis is therefore necessary for the "entirely an artifact" conclusion. That gives the authors a stake in rejecting it beyond the statistical weakness they cite.

## 5. Smaller points

- **Record-based output isn't automatically better.** One of the record types listed is *billable hours delivered*. That measures time worked, not output, so it falls automatically when hours are cut. If some of the 23 record-based indices rest on billable hours, the 3.8-point gap partly reflects a weakness in the records, not just optimistic managers. The comparison should be broken down by type of record.
- **Comparing retail with Varden's counter offices is suggestive but thin.** The retail figure comes from three organisations and a different measure (an output index, not Varden's difference-in-differences estimate of output per employee). The near match of −11.2% and −11.4% is suggestive but could be coincidental.
- **The real-revenue figure has no comparison group.** The −2.6% is correctly calculated, but without a comparison group it can't be attributed to the pilot. The authors partly acknowledge this when they call revenue a poor proxy.
- **No uncertainty is reported** for any of the corrected estimates.

## Conclusion

The defensible version of this comment would say the following:

- Halden's 23.4% is substantially overstated.
- Correcting output and hours in the subset where that is possible cuts the gain to about 11%.
- Attrition and novelty could reduce it further, by amounts not yet measured.
- In coverage-bound work, reduced hours reduce output.

All of that is well supported and useful.

What isn't supported is "entirely an artifact". The comment's own numbers and Varden's randomised case-processing result both point to a smaller but real per-hour gain in backlog-type work. The most useful additions would be:

1. the monthly-trajectory test of the novelty argument;
2. bounds for attrition;
3. a reconciliation of the hours components;
4. a breakdown of the record-based output measures by type.
